Our World: The week of Nov. 9, 2026
Our World is a roundup from our weekly print edition of noteworthy happenings, from our global correspondents and editors.
“A lot of excitement and a lot of wow”
That’s NASA astrophysicist Tom Statler, speaking about a quest to bring the first samples back from one of Mars’ moons. A Japanese spacecraft set off Oct. 20 on the five-year mission that will attempt to land a robotic prospector and a rover on Phobos, the larger of Mars’ two moons. Five space agencies have joined forces. If successful, dust, soil, and rocks from Phobos will arrive on Earth in 2031. 
– Tim Backshall  
Veterans make gains in Russia’s State Duma 
About 10% of new deputies of Russia’s freshly elected State Duma, the 450-seat lower house of parliament, are veterans of the war with Ukraine. Their political advancement is a sign that the Kremlin’s Time of Heroes program, which supports soldiers returning from the front lines, is taking effect. Russians recall the cycle of poverty, crime, and social dysfunction that beset men coming home from the Afghan war in the 1980s, and to avoid such problems, the new veterans will receive a range of official assistance and benefits. Most of the elected veterans were put forward by the pro-Kremlin United Russia party. – Fred Weir 
Black-led African firms struggle to find funding
Despite three decades of affirmative action policies, about two-thirds of South Africa’s largest businesses are led and owned by people other than its Black majority, according to a recent study by British International Investment, the United Kingdom’s development finance institution. This reflects a wider trend. Across Africa, companies with Black founders struggle to find funding in order to expand. Between 2000 and 2024, only 3% of investment into startups in Africa went to companies with Black founders, according to the Google for Startups Black Founders Fund. –  Ryan Lenora Brown
Indian immigrants opt for EU over US
Indians are increasingly moving to the European Union, while their pace of immigration to the United States and Canada is slowing. The shift comes amid signs of labor shortages in the EU, especially in categories such as electrical engineers and nurses, according to the Japanese media outlet Nikkei Asia. India and the EU concluded a labor mobility agreement in January. In a parallel trend, some European countries, such as Germany, are seeing a growing influx of Indian students, while their numbers are decreasing in the U.S. and Canada, Nikkei says. – Ann Scott Tyson
